title: What Is the Ideal Team Size for Getting Things Done?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Citing team research that groups of 4-6 make higher-quality decisions, the piece argues that the trend toward inclusive leadership has swollen team sizes and diluted their ability to get things done. Rather than trading inclusion against effectiveness, the authors propose using both: larger teams for updating, brainstorming, discussing and debating, which builds ownership and engagement as long as everyone can still be heard. Specific tasks and decisions, however, should go to hand-picked temporary work teams of 4-6 people chosen for diverse views and directly relevant skills. These teams differ from task forces because members are selected for expertise, not to represent the larger group, and they may tackle several assignments together. The guiding question for leaders is which composition of 4-6 people gives the best chance of excellence on a given task.
points: Research favors teams of 4-6 for decision quality, and the drift toward inclusive, larger teams has eroded execution.
Inclusion and effectiveness need not be traded off: use large teams for discussion and engagement, small teams for tasks and decisions.
Small work teams should be hand-selected for task-relevant skills and diverse views, not as representatives of the larger group.
The practical question is which specific 4-6 people give the best chance to achieve a task with excellence.
quotes: Team research continues to affirm the fact that smaller teams outperform larger teams. Teams of 4-6 people make higher-quality decisions and address issues more effectively.
Teams with more members fulfill the need to create a more inclusive work culture but undermine the ability of those teams to achieve quality outcomes and decisions.
As long as a team does not expand beyond the size where everyone can be heard and make their view known in a meeting, larger teams galvanize the commitment team members have for the organization.

But good leaders don’t ask larger teams to achieve specific tasks or decisions. Instead, they clearly delineate the assignment and create a temporary work team made up of team members with the right skills to tackle it.
More importantly, the members should not be representative of a larger team but selected specifically for their unique skills or expertise related to the challenge.
Weaving the synergies between large and small teams is commonplace for the best leaders. They include more people in the conversation while getting important things done in smaller teams.
